playbooks.name: thesis
playbooks.label: Thesis / Dissertation
playbooks.summary: A long-form original study with a question, a method, evidence and a defensible conclusion. The heaviest thing on this list, and the one that carries most weight on a CV when it is actually finished.
playbooks.outcome_label: A 50–90 page bound thesis, plus a defence

formats.name: Abstract
formats.detail: The whole study in one paragraph: question, method, finding, implication. Written last, read first.

formats.name: Introduction
formats.detail: The question, why it matters, and what you will and will not cover.

formats.name: Literature review
formats.detail: What is already settled, what is contested, and the gap you are filling. Organised by theme, never as a list of summaries.

formats.name: Methodology
formats.detail: What you did, in enough detail that someone else could repeat it. Includes sampling, instruments and limitations.

formats.name: Results
formats.detail: What you found, with no interpretation. Tables and figures carry this section.

formats.name: Discussion & conclusion
formats.detail: What it means, where it disagrees with the literature, what you would do next.

formats.name: References & appendices
formats.detail: One citation style, applied consistently. Instruments, raw tables and code go in appendices.

dos: Pick a question narrow enough to answer with data you can genuinely obtain. Scope is the single biggest cause of unfinished theses.
Write the question as one sentence and show it to your supervisor before anything else.
Start the citation manager on day one, with every paper you read, including the ones you discard.
Keep a decisions log: every scope change, every dropped variable, with the date and the reason. Your methodology chapter is this log, rewritten.
Write the methodology while you are doing the method, not six weeks later from memory.
Agree the exact submission format and deadline with your department in writing, early.
donts: Don't start by writing Chapter 1. Start by writing the question and the method.
Don't collect data before the method is settled and, where relevant, approved — unapproved data can be unusable.
Don't review literature by summarising paper after paper. Group by argument; a reader wants the state of the debate, not your reading list.
Don't put interpretation in Results or new results in Discussion. Examiners notice immediately.
Don't leave formatting, numbering and the reference list to the final week. It reliably takes days, not hours.

exports.detail: A link to a repository with a DOI makes the study checkable.
exports.how: Deposit on Zenodo or OSF and cite the DOI in the thesis.

playbooks.name: mvp
playbooks.label: MVP / Product Build
playbooks.summary: The smallest thing you can put in front of real users that proves one idea. Ships with a repo, a README and numbers — the evidence that turns "I can build" into something a reviewer can check.
playbooks.cv_line: <Product> — built and shipped an MVP used by <N> users; <the one metric that moved>
playbooks.outcome_label: A working build with real users and a public repo

formats.name: One-line pitch
formats.detail: Who it's for, what it does, why now. If this takes a paragraph, the scope is wrong.

formats.name: Problem statement
formats.detail: The job the user is trying to do today, and what it costs them. Evidence from interviews, not intuition.

formats.name: Spec / PRD
formats.detail: The one job the MVP does, what is explicitly out of scope, and the acceptance criteria.

formats.name: The build
formats.detail: A thin working slice, not a skeleton of everything. One path, end to end, that actually works.

formats.name: README
formats.detail: What it is, a screenshot or demo link, how to run it, what's next, the licence.

formats.name: Results note
formats.detail: Users, the metric, what you learned, what you'd change. This is what makes it a CV line.

dos: Talk to five real users before writing any code, and write down what they said in their words.
Pick the one job the product does and write the other ideas on a visibly separate out-of-scope list.
Build the thin slice: one complete path that works, rather than a shell of every screen.
Instrument it before launch — sign-ups, the one action that matters, and retention after a week. Numbers are what a CV line is made of.
Ship a README with a screenshot or a live link. Most reviewers decide from the README alone.
Add a licence. Without one nobody may legally reuse it, including someone evaluating you.
donts: Don't build authentication, billing and an admin panel before anyone has used the core feature once.
Don't call a landing page an MVP. An MVP is used; a landing page is read.
Don't skip the metric because the numbers are small. Five engaged users is a finding; "it works" is not.
Don't leave the repo private and the demo dead. An unreachable project is an unverifiable claim.
Don't take a feature request from the loudest user as a priority. One user is an anecdote.

exports.how: Deploy to a free host and check the link from a logged-out browser.

exports.detail: 90 seconds, no voice needed. Survives the demo being down.

exports.how: Export as PDF; link it from both the repo and your CV.

playbooks.name: research
playbooks.label: Research Study
playbooks.summary: A standalone empirical study — survey, interviews or desk research — run properly enough that someone can act on the answer. Lighter than a thesis, and the same discipline.
playbooks.cv_line: Research study: <question> — <method, N>; findings used to <decision it informed>
playbooks.outcome_label: A 10–20 page research report with a defensible method

formats.name: Executive summary
formats.detail: The answer first, in three bullets, for a reader who stops there.

formats.name: Question & scope
formats.detail: What you asked, and the decision it is meant to inform.

formats.name: Method
formats.detail: Design, sample, instrument, dates, limitations. Reproducible by a stranger.

formats.name: Findings
formats.detail: One finding per section, each with its evidence. Charts carry the weight.

formats.name: Implications
formats.detail: So what, and for whom. The section that stops it being trivia.

formats.name: Appendix
formats.detail: Full instrument, response tables, and the raw data or a link to it.

dos: Write the decision the study informs before you write the question. A study nobody will act on is a hobby.
Decide the analysis before collecting the data, and write it down somewhere dated.
Pilot the survey or interview guide on five people and expect to rewrite a third of it.
Report your N, your response rate and who you could not reach. Credibility lives in the limitations.
Quote participants verbatim. Paraphrase is where findings quietly become opinions.
donts: Don't write leading questions. "How much do you value X?" has already assumed the answer.
Don't mix a 1–5 scale with a 1–7 scale across the same instrument.
Don't claim significance from 30 convenience responses. Say what it is: indicative.
Don't bury the answer on page nine. Executive summary first, always.
Don't delete inconvenient responses. Report them, and say why they are inconvenient.

exports.detail: Eight to ten slides for people who will not read the report.
exports.how: One finding per slide, the chart as the hero, the claim as the title.

exports.detail: Anonymised responses, so the analysis is checkable.
exports.how: Strip identifiers, publish as CSV on OSF or Zenodo, cite the DOI.

playbooks.name: report
playbooks.label: Business / Consulting Report
playbooks.summary: A recommendation someone can act on, with the analysis behind it. The most reusable deliverable on this list — the same structure carries an internal memo, a client report and a course submission.
playbooks.cv_line: <Topic> report for <org/course> — recommended <X>; <what was adopted or what it quantified>
playbooks.outcome_label: A 10–15 page report or a 15-slide deck with a clear recommendation

formats.name: Executive summary
formats.detail: The recommendation, the three reasons, the ask. One page, readable standing up.

formats.name: Situation & question
formats.detail: What is happening, and the specific question the report answers.

formats.name: Analysis
formats.detail: One argument per section, each with the numbers under it.

formats.name: Recommendation
formats.detail: One recommendation. Alternatives considered and why they lose.

formats.name: Risks & next steps
formats.detail: What could go wrong, and who does what by when.

formats.name: Appendix
formats.detail: Model, assumptions, sources. Everything a sceptic would want to check.

dos: Answer first. Lead with the recommendation and let the reader stop reading whenever they are convinced.
Make every section title a claim, not a label: "Margin is falling because of mix, not price" beats "Margin analysis".
Put the assumptions in a single visible table. Reviewers attack hidden assumptions and accept stated ones.
Quantify the recommendation. "Save ₹40L a year" survives a meeting; "improve efficiency" does not.
Give one recommendation. Three options with no pick is a decision handed back to the reader.
donts: Don't build suspense. This is not an essay; the conclusion goes first.
Don't present a framework as a finding. SWOT is how you thought, not what you concluded.
Don't use a chart you cannot explain in one sentence.
Don't hide the weak assumption in a footnote. Someone will find it, and then the whole report is suspect.
Don't deliver without a next step. A report with no ask does not get acted on.

formats.name: Question
formats.detail: One sentence, answerable from the data you have.

formats.name: Data note
formats.detail: Source, licence, period, row count, and what each column means.

formats.name: Cleaning log
formats.detail: Every transformation, in order, re-runnable. The difference between an analysis and a guess.

formats.name: Analysis
formats.detail: The exploration, the test, and the result — including what you expected and did not find.

formats.name: Dashboard or notebook
formats.detail: The interactive artifact. Readable by someone who was not there.

formats.name: One-page write-up
formats.detail: Question, method, finding, caveat. What you actually send someone.

dos: Check the licence before you use a dataset. A portfolio piece built on data you had no right to use is unusable.
Profile every column before analysing anything — distinct values, blanks, ranges, impossible numbers.
Keep the raw file untouched and do every transformation in Power Query, SQL or a script you can re-run.
Write down what you expected before you look. Otherwise every result confirms what you already thought.
State the finding with a number and a caveat in the same sentence.
donts: Don't clean by typing over cells. An untraceable fix is an untrustworthy analysis.
Don't present correlation as cause. Name the confounder you cannot rule out.
Don't build twelve charts. Build the two that answer the question and delete the rest.
Don't leave a dashboard with no title, no date, and no source. Nobody will trust it and nobody will ask.
Don't drop the outliers because they are inconvenient. Investigate them — they are often the finding.

playbooks.name: case
playbooks.label: Case Competition Entry
playbooks.summary: A judged recommendation under a deadline. Compressed version of the consulting report, with the scoring rubric as the spec and a Q&A you cannot prepare slides for.
playbooks.cv_line: <Competition> — <placement> of <N> teams; recommended <X> backed by a <model type>
playbooks.outcome_label: A 10–15 slide deck, a model, and a rehearsed Q&A

formats.name: Title slide
formats.detail: The recommendation as the title. Judges have read twenty decks; lead with the answer.

formats.name: Situation
formats.detail: What is true today, in numbers, in one slide.

formats.name: Recommendation
formats.detail: One recommendation, quantified, with the three reasons.

formats.name: Supporting analysis
formats.detail: Market size, financials, competitive angle. One claim per slide.

formats.name: Implementation
formats.detail: Phases, owners, timeline. Judges mark this and teams skip it.

formats.name: Risks & appendix
formats.detail: The three risks with mitigations, and the model behind the numbers.

dos: Read the rubric and build the deck against it. The rubric is the spec, and most teams never open it.
Answer the question actually asked, including the parts that are inconvenient for your idea.
Quantify the recommendation. A judged recommendation without a number loses to one with a rough number.
Put implementation in. It is usually 15–20% of the marks and routinely left out.
Rehearse the handoffs between speakers. Judges see unpractised transitions as unpractised thinking.
donts: Don't present three options and no choice. The decision is what is being marked.
Don't fill slides with frameworks. A Porter's Five Forces slide with no conclusion is a wasted slide.
Don't invent numbers. State assumptions and sources; a judge will ask where a figure came from.
Don't overrun. Being cut off before your recommendation is the worst outcome available.
Don't let one person answer every question. Judges are marking the team.

playbooks.name: model
playbooks.label: Financial Model
playbooks.summary: A working, auditable model of one real company or decision — historicals from filings, a forecast someone can argue with, and a valuation that survives having its assumptions changed in front of you.
playbooks.cv_line: Built a <model type> for <company/decision> — <the number it produced, and what it changed>
playbooks.outcome_label: An auditable workbook plus a one-page output

formats.name: Cover and contents
formats.detail: What the model is, as of when, in what units, and who built it. The first thing a reviewer looks for and the thing most models omit.

formats.name: Inputs tab
formats.detail: Every hardcoded assumption in one place, coloured blue, each with its source.

formats.name: Workings
formats.detail: Calculations in dated columns, one consistent timeline across every sheet, logic flowing left to right and top to bottom.

formats.name: Outputs
formats.detail: The statements, the valuation and the sensitivities a reader actually looks at.

formats.name: Control / checks tab
formats.detail: Balance-sheet check, cash-flow tie, and a flag that goes red when any of them break.

formats.name: One-page summary
formats.detail: The answer, the three assumptions it depends on, and the range. For the person who will not open the workbook.

dos: Separate inputs, calculations and outputs, and colour them so a stranger can tell which is which at a glance.
Keep one timeline across every sheet: the same period in the same column, everywhere, without exception.
Write every formula in a row identically across the whole row — one exception in one column is how models get silently wrong.
Put a checks tab in on day one: balance-sheet check, cash tie, and sum-of-parts ties. Make failures red and visible.
Source every hardcoded number next to the cell. A number with no source is an opinion.
Build the historicals before the forecast. The forecast's job is to be consistent with what already happened.
donts: Don't hardcode a number inside a formula. It is invisible there and it will be wrong later.
Don't use OFFSET or INDIRECT — they break auditing tools and nobody can trace them.
Don't link to another workbook. The link will break, usually in front of someone senior.
Don't build ten years of forecast. Nobody believes year seven, and defending it wastes the review.
Don't leave iterative calculation on as the fix for circularity — add a circuit breaker you can switch off.
Don't hide rows or sheets to tidy up. Group them, so a reviewer can see there is something there.

formats.detail: Company, what it does in one sentence, and the ask. A reader should be able to repeat it after one look.

formats.name: Problem
formats.detail: Who has it, what it costs them, and what they do today instead. Evidence, not assertion.

formats.name: Solution and product
formats.detail: What you built, shown rather than described — a screenshot beats three bullets.

formats.name: Why now
formats.detail: What changed that makes this possible or necessary this year. The slide most decks skip and most investors ask about.

formats.name: Market
formats.detail: Built bottom-up with your assumptions visible. A top-down "1% of a $50B market" slide reads as a red flag.

formats.name: Traction
formats.detail: The chart that goes up, with its axis labelled and its period stated. If it is small, say it is early.

formats.name: Business model and unit economics
formats.detail: What you charge, what it costs to serve, and what a customer is worth.

formats.name: Team
formats.detail: Why these people, for this problem. Relevant specifics only.

formats.name: The ask
formats.detail: How much, for what runway, and the three things it buys. Broken down, not a single number.

formats.name: Appendix
formats.detail: Cohorts, pipeline, the model, the competitive detail. Where the hard questions get answered.

dos: Write the narrative as ten sentences before you open a slide tool. If the sentences do not follow each other, no amount of design fixes it.
Make every slide title a claim: "Retention holds at 62% in month six" beats "Retention".
Build the market bottom-up and show the arithmetic on the slide.
Put one idea on each slide and let the chart carry it.
Break the ask down into what it buys — headcount, runway, a specific milestone.
Keep an appendix for everything you cut, and know which slide answers which question.
donts: Don't open with the team or the agenda. Open with what the company does.
Don't show a hockey-stick projection with no mechanism behind it.
Don't claim no competition. It reads as not having looked.
Don't put more than about thirty words on a slide you intend to talk over.
Don't quote a market size you cannot derive on the spot.
Don't send a deck that needs you to narrate it — most decks are read, not presented.

playbooks.summary: Take one recurring manual task and make it run itself — the smallest project on this list, the fastest to finish, and the easiest to put a saved-hours number against on a CV.
playbooks.cv_line: Automated <task> — removed <N> hours a week of manual work across <team>
playbooks.outcome_label: A live automation with a documented handover

formats.name: Before map
formats.detail: The manual process as it runs today: every step, who does it, how long it takes, how often.

formats.name: After map
formats.detail: The same process with the automated steps marked and the human decision points left in.

formats.name: The automation
formats.detail: The live workflow — trigger, steps, filters, error path.

formats.name: Failure handling
formats.detail: What happens when a step fails, who finds out, and how it is retried.

formats.name: Handover note
formats.detail: How to run it, change it and switch it off. Without this it dies when you leave.

formats.name: Saved-time measurement
formats.detail: Before and after, measured not estimated. This is the CV line.

dos: Time the manual task before you automate it. Without a before, there is no after.
Map the process on paper first — half the steps turn out to be unnecessary rather than automatable.
Automate the boring majority and leave the judgement calls to a person.
Make failures loud: a message to a channel someone reads, not a silent log.
Run it alongside the manual process for a week before switching the manual one off.
Write the handover note while you build, not afterwards.
donts: Don't automate a process nobody has agreed on. You will encode one person's version of it.
Don't let it fail silently. A broken automation that looks fine is worse than no automation.
Don't hardcode credentials into a step. Use the tool's own secret store.
Don't give it write access to anything it does not need, and never to production records on day one.
Don't build a twelve-step workflow first. Build three steps that work, then extend.
Don't skip the saved-hours measurement — it is the entire reason this is a CV line.

formats.detail: What the room can do at the end that they could not at the start. A verb, not a topic.

formats.name: Run sheet
formats.detail: Minute-by-minute: segment, who talks, what the room does, how long. The document you actually hold.

formats.name: Materials
formats.detail: Slides if needed, and the worksheet or template the room works on. The worksheet matters more.

formats.name: Exercise brief
formats.detail: The task the room does, written so it needs no further explanation from you.

formats.name: Takeaway
formats.detail: The one-page thing they leave with and will actually use next week.

formats.name: Feedback form
formats.detail: Three questions, collected before anyone leaves the room.

dos: Write the objective as something the room can DO, then design backwards from it.
Give at least half the time to the room doing something, not to you talking.
Write the exercise brief so it is self-explanatory — if you have to clarify it live, it is not finished.
Pilot it on two or three people and expect to cut a quarter of the content.
Prepare for the technology failing: a printed run sheet and a version that works with no screen.
Collect feedback in the room. Nobody fills in the form you email afterwards.
donts: Don't build forty slides. A slide count that high means you are lecturing, not running a workshop.
Don't open with a round of introductions in a large room — it eats the first twenty minutes.
Don't demonstrate the whole thing and then ask them to try it. Alternate small chunks.
Don't leave the exercise open-ended. A specific, bounded task produces better work than "discuss".
Don't skip timing the segments. Overrunning is the failure mode of every first workshop.
Don't end on questions. End on what they will do differently, in writing.

tools.name: Atlassian Team Playbook
tools.use: Free ready-made workshop formats with timings and materials

tools.name: Google Slides / Docs
tools.use: Materials and the worksheet the room works on

tools.name: Miro / FigJam
tools.use: A shared board for remote sessions; free tiers cover a single workshop

tools.name: Google Forms
tools.use: A three-question feedback form, with a CSV you can quote from

exports.name: Run sheet
exports.detail: The timed plan, and the artifact that proves you designed rather than improvised.
exports.how: A table: time, segment, who, what the room does. Print it.

exports.name: Materials pack
exports.detail: Slides, worksheet and brief, in a form someone else could run.
exports.how: One folder or PDF, with the run sheet first.

exports.name: Takeaway one-pager
exports.detail: What the room leaves with. Often the only thing they keep.
exports.how: Export to PDF and hand it out on paper as well as by link.

exports.name: Feedback summary
exports.detail: What they said, including what did not work. Quote it on your CV only if it is real.
exports.how: Export the form responses and write three lines on what you would change.

stages.title: Narrow the question until it is answerable
stages.description: Most theses fail here, months before anyone notices. A good question is one sentence, has a method attached, and names the data you can actually get.

checklist.d: If it needs two sentences it is two questions. Pick one.

checklist.t: Name the method in the same breath
checklist.d: "...measured by a survey of 200 X" or "...by regression on Y panel data". A question with no method is a topic, not a question.
Find and open the actual dataset, or confirm you can reach the actual people. Do this before committing.

checklist.t: Write the limitation you already know about
checklist.d: Every design has one. Naming it now stops it being a surprise in the viva.
One sentence, one method, one data source, in an email to your supervisor.

stages.title: Review the literature without drowning in it
stages.description: You are mapping a debate, not reading everything. Twenty well-chosen papers organised by argument beats a hundred summarised in sequence.

checklist.d: Find the three most-cited works on your question and mine their reference lists both directions.

checklist.t: Log every paper in Zotero as you read
checklist.d: Title, the one-line finding, and whether you agree. Retro-fitting this costs days.

checklist.t: Group by argument, not by author
checklist.d: Build a table: position, who holds it, on what evidence. That table becomes your chapter structure.

checklist.t: Write the gap in two sentences
checklist.d: "Everyone agrees X. Nobody has tested it on Y." That is your contribution.

stages.title: Design the method, in writing, before touching data
stages.description: Sampling, instrument, variables and the analysis you will run. Written down and dated — this is the chapter that makes the study credible or not.

checklist.t: Define the population and the sample
checklist.d: Who exactly, how many, and recruited how. Convenience sampling is acceptable if you say so.
Every survey question or interview prompt, written out. Then cut a third of them.
You will find two broken questions. Always.
Name the test before you see the data. This is what separates a finding from a fishing trip.

checklist.t: Clear ethics or approval if required
checklist.d: Human subjects usually need it, and it usually takes longer than you think.

stages.title: Collect and clean the data
stages.description: The unglamorous half of the calendar. Keep the raw file untouched and do every transformation in a script or a query you can re-run.

checklist.d: Never edit the original export. Every cleaning step happens on a copy, reproducibly.
Rows dropped, why, and how many. The examiner will ask about your N.
Distinct values, blanks, impossible numbers. Find the data-entry errors before they become findings.
Started with X, excluded Y for reason Z, analysed N. One table.

stages.title: Run the analysis you planned
stages.description: The plan from stage 3, executed. Exploratory extras are fine — label them exploratory.

checklist.d: Before anything else, so you cannot talk yourself into a different one.

checklist.t: Report effect size, not just significance
checklist.d: A significant result that is tiny is a finding about your sample size.

checklist.t: Produce the tables and figures now
checklist.d: Numbered, captioned, readable in black and white. These are the Results chapter.
Honest and costs you nothing. Hiding it costs you the viva.

stages.title: Write the chapters in the order that works
stages.description: Methodology, then Results, then Discussion, then Introduction, then Abstract last. Writing the introduction first is why so many drafts contradict their own findings.

checklist.t: Use Word styles from the first page
checklist.d: Heading 1/2/3 only. Your contents page, numbering and PDF bookmarks all come free.
They are the most factual and the least negotiable. Momentum comes from these.
Each finding: what it means, who it agrees with, who it contradicts.
Now you know what the thesis actually says.
References, figure numbering, margins, pagination. Book two days for this.

stages.title: Defend it
stages.description: A viva tests whether you understand your own limitations. Preparing the attacks yourself is the whole technique.

checklist.t: Write the five hardest questions yourself
checklist.d: Start with your own limitations section. The examiner will.
Question, method, finding, limitation, next step. Not a tour of the document.

checklist.t: Be able to defend the sample
checklist.d: Why this N, why these people, what it does and does not generalise to.
Twice. Reading it silently does not count.

stages.title: Find a problem worth solving
stages.description: Five conversations before any code. You are listening for what people already do and what it costs them — not for whether they like your idea.

checklist.t: Interview five people in the target group
checklist.d: Ask what they did last time, not what they would do. Past behaviour is evidence; intent is not.
Verbatim quotes. Your summary of what they meant is already your bias.
Everyone has one — a spreadsheet, a WhatsApp group, doing nothing. That is your real competitor.

checklist.t: State the cost of the problem
checklist.d: Hours, rupees, or errors per week. No measurable cost, no product.

stages.title: Cut the scope to one job
stages.description: Write the out-of-scope list where you can see it. Scope creep is the only reason most MVPs never ship.

checklist.d: For <user>, <product> does <one job>. If it needs an "and", cut something.

checklist.t: List everything you are not building
checklist.d: Explicitly, in the spec. This list is what protects your timeline.
One sentence describing a user completing the job end to end. That is v1.

checklist.t: Set a ship date and keep it
checklist.d: Scope flexes to fit the date, not the other way round.

stages.title: Write the spec
stages.description: One or two pages: the job, the flow, the acceptance criteria, the out-of-scope list. It exists so you stop re-deciding things at 1am.

checklist.t: Describe the happy path as numbered steps
checklist.d: From landing to the job being done. Count the steps — then remove two.
"A new user can do X in under Y seconds without help." Testable, not aspirational.
The action that means the product worked. Pick it now, before it is convenient to pick a flattering one.
Especially anything personal. Decide now what you do not collect.

stages.title: Prototype before you build
stages.description: A clickable prototype costs a day and finds the flow problems that cost a week in code.

checklist.d: Three or four screens. Empty states and errors come later.
Link the screens so someone can walk the flow without you narrating.
Silently. Where they hesitate is where your build will fail.

checklist.t: Fix the flow, then stop designing
checklist.d: The prototype's job is done the moment the flow stops confusing people.

stages.title: Build the thin slice
stages.description: One complete path that genuinely works, deployed somewhere a stranger can reach. No auth, billing or admin until the core job works.

checklist.d: An empty deployed app beats a perfect local one. Everything after is a small change to something live.
Resist every edge case until the main path works end to end.

checklist.t: Use managed services for the boring parts
checklist.d: Auth, database, file storage. Writing your own is a project, not a feature.
A reviewer reads your commit history as evidence of how you work.

stages.title: Put it in front of five users
stages.description: Watch them use it without helping. Everything you want to explain is a thing the product should have said.

checklist.t: Give a task, not a tour
checklist.d: "Do X." Then stay quiet, however painful it gets.
Where they pause, re-read or click the wrong thing. That list is your backlog.
How many finished the task unaided? That number is your first real result.
Preferences are noise at this stage; blockers are not.

stages.title: Instrument it and read the numbers
stages.description: Without a metric you have an anecdote. With one you have a CV line someone can ask you about.

checklist.t: Track sign-up, the core action, and week-one return
checklist.d: Three events. More than that and you will not look at any of them.
Week one's numbers, written down, before you start improving things.

checklist.t: Make one change and measure it
checklist.d: One change, one measurement. Two at once teaches you nothing.
"11 of 18 returned in week one." Specific and modest beats vague and grand.

stages.title: Package it so a reviewer can verify it
stages.description: The build is not the deliverable; the verifiable build is. README, screenshot, live link, licence, one-page case study.

checklist.d: What it is, a screenshot, the demo link, how to run it, the licence. In that order.
MIT unless you have a reason. No licence means nobody may legally reuse it.
Insurance against the live link being down the day someone looks.
Problem, build, numbers, learning. This is what goes in the CV entry.

stages.title: Frame the question and the decision behind it
stages.description: Name the decision the answer changes. If nothing changes either way, the study is not worth running.

checklist.d: "We will do A or B depending on this." Then write the question that separates A from B.

checklist.t: State what would change your mind
checklist.d: The result that would make you conclude the opposite. Name it now.
Which population, which period, which geography. Write down what is excluded.

stages.title: Choose primary or secondary — and don't collect what exists
stages.description: Most questions are partly answered already. Finding that out costs a day and can save three weeks.

checklist.d: Dataset search, official statistics, published industry reports.

checklist.t: Decide what genuinely needs primary collection
checklist.d: Usually a narrow slice, not the whole question.
Who collected it, when, how, and with what incentive.

stages.title: Design the instrument
stages.description: Survey questions or an interview guide, written out in full, then cut by a third. Long instruments produce abandoned ones.

checklist.d: Then delete any that will not change a conclusion.
Pick 1–5 or 1–7 and keep it throughout.
Read each one aloud and ask whether it implies its own answer.
Time it. Note which questions they ask you to explain, and rewrite those.

stages.title: Sample it so the answer means something
stages.description: Who you asked decides what the answer is worth. A convenience sample is fine if you say so and reason accordingly.

checklist.d: The group the answer is about, precisely.

checklist.t: Choose the sampling method and name it
checklist.d: Random, stratified, convenience, snowball. Each has a known weakness — state yours.

checklist.t: Work out the N you need
checklist.d: And if you cannot reach it, decide in advance how you will caveat the result.
Who is systematically missing, and which way that biases the finding.

stages.title: Run it
stages.description: Fieldwork. Keep the log as you go — dates, counts, anything odd that happened.

checklist.d: Dates, invitations sent, responses in, dropouts. Your method section needs these numbers.
With consent. Quoting from memory is how findings drift.
Every clarification you give is a question you should have written better.

checklist.t: Stop when you said you would
checklist.d: Extending the window to chase a nicer number is a bias, not diligence.

stages.title: Analyse and test what you think you found
stages.description: Run the planned analysis, then look for the explanation that would make your finding wrong.

checklist.d: Incomplete responses, straight-lining, impossible answers. Count them.
Then anything exploratory, clearly labelled as such.
Usually the finding is about a subgroup, not the population.

checklist.t: Write each finding as a sentence with a number in it
checklist.d: If you cannot put a number in it, it is an impression.

stages.title: Write the report
stages.description: Answer first, method second, evidence third. Written for someone who will read the first page and the charts.

checklist.t: Write the executive summary as three bullets
checklist.d: Each one a finding with a number. Write this last and put it first.
Section title states the finding; the body is its evidence.
Title says the point, axes labelled, source noted. A chart needing narration will be misread.
Sample, method, period. This section is why a reader trusts the rest.

stages.title: Get the question right
stages.description: Most bad reports answer a question nobody asked. Write the question down and have it confirmed before you analyse anything.

checklist.t: Write the question as a decision
checklist.d: "Should we do X?" or "Which of X/Y?" — not "an analysis of the market".
Each answerable with data. These become your analysis sections.
What you expect the answer to be, so you notice when the data disagrees.
In writing. Scope disputes at the end are fatal; at the start they are free.

stages.title: Structure the answer before gathering anything
stages.description: Write the storyline first — the recommendation and the three reasons — then go find out whether it is true. It tells you exactly what to research.

checklist.d: Recommendation, three supporting claims, the evidence each one needs.

checklist.t: Write every section title as a claim
checklist.d: If a title could sit on any report, it is a label, not a claim.

checklist.t: List the evidence you need per claim
checklist.d: This is your research plan, and it stops you reading indefinitely.
The data will change the storyline once. If it never does, you were not testing anything.

stages.title: Do the research
stages.description: Targeted at the claims in the storyline. Record the source of every number as you take it, not afterwards.

checklist.t: Start with official and industry sources
checklist.d: Regulators, annual reports, industry associations. Cite upstream, not a blog quoting them.

checklist.t: Log every figure with its source and date
checklist.d: One sheet: number, source, URL, date. You will need this for the appendix.
A number your recommendation depends on needs two independent sources.

checklist.t: Note what you could not find
checklist.d: A named gap is a limitation; an unnamed one reads as an error.

stages.title: Build the numbers
stages.description: A small, auditable model: inputs separated from calculations, assumptions visible, sensitivities run.

checklist.d: Three visually distinct blocks. Blue inputs, black formulas.

checklist.t: Put every assumption on one tab
checklist.d: With its source. This is the first tab a reviewer opens.
Flex the two assumptions that matter most and show the range, not a single point.
Is the answer the right order of magnitude against a known benchmark? Most model errors are 10x errors.

stages.title: Write the recommendation
stages.description: One recommendation, quantified, with the alternatives named and dismissed on stated grounds.

checklist.t: State it in one sentence with a number
checklist.d: "Exit the B segment; it costs ₹1.2Cr a year at a 4% share."
Each traceable to a section of your analysis.

checklist.t: Name the alternatives and why they lose
checklist.d: Shows you considered them, and pre-empts the obvious challenge.
What you want decided, by whom, by when.

stages.title: Make the slides
stages.description: The deck is the same argument, not a summary of the document. Action titles, one idea per slide.

checklist.d: The title is the takeaway. Read the titles in sequence — they should tell the whole story.
Two ideas means two slides, or one of them is not needed.

checklist.t: Let the chart be the slide
checklist.d: Highlight the one bar or line that makes the point; grey the rest.

checklist.t: Put the detail in an appendix
checklist.d: Available when challenged, not in the flow.

stages.title: Present it and survive the questions
stages.description: You will get between five and ten minutes before the first interruption. Plan for the interruption.

checklist.d: Not the agenda, not the methodology. The answer.
Start with your weakest assumption — that is where the first question lands.

checklist.t: Know your numbers without the slides
checklist.d: Being unable to recall your own figure undoes the whole report.
Restate what you need decided, and write down what was decided.

stages.title: Scope a question and find data you may legally use
stages.description: Both halves matter. The licence check is thirty seconds and saves a portfolio piece you cannot show.

checklist.t: Write the question as one sentence
checklist.d: Specific enough that a number answers it.
Open it. Count the rows. Check the columns you need actually exist.
Who may use it, for what. Note it in your data note.
Source, period, rows, columns and their meanings. Future-you will not remember.

stages.title: Profile and clean it, reproducibly
stages.description: Where the time actually goes. Every fix happens in a step you can re-run, never by typing over a cell.

checklist.d: Read-only copy. Everything downstream is derived.
Distinct values, blanks, min/max, type. Find the "-999" that means missing.
Power Query, SQL or script. Delete-and-retype is not a cleaning step.

checklist.t: Log the row count at each stage
checklist.d: Started X, dropped Y because Z, left with N.

stages.title: Shape it into something you can analyse
stages.description: One row per observation, one column per variable, one header row. Most analysis pain is a shape problem.

checklist.t: Get it to one row per observation
checklist.d: Unpivot wide data. Columns named 2019, 2020, 2021 are values, not fields.

checklist.t: Join in the lookups you need
checklist.d: Categories, regions, dates. Check the row count did not change after each join.
A real date, not text. Half of all analysis bugs are date bugs.

checklist.t: Save the query, not the result
checklist.d: So next month's file runs through the same pipeline untouched.

stages.title: Explore it before you test anything
stages.description: Look at the distributions first. The question you can answer is often not the one you arrived with.

checklist.d: Before you look. This is the only way to notice a result that is merely flattering.

checklist.t: Plot every variable you care about
checklist.d: Distribution and over time. Bimodal data means two populations.
Error, or the most interesting thing in the dataset? Find out which.
Honest and common. Record that you did and why.

stages.title: Test what you think you found
stages.description: A difference you can see is not yet a difference that exists. Name the confounder you cannot rule out.

checklist.t: Pick the test before running it
checklist.d: Match it to the data you have, not to the answer you want.
Significant and trivial is a sentence about your sample size.
Usually the effect lives in one subgroup. Say so.

checklist.t: Write the caveat in the same sentence as the finding
checklist.d: "X is 12% higher, though the Y segment is under-represented."

stages.title: Build the dashboard
stages.description: Two or three charts that answer the question, titled so they read without you in the room.

checklist.t: Answer the question in the top-left
checklist.d: The headline number, with its period. Everything else is support.

checklist.t: Keep it to two or three charts
checklist.d: Each must earn its place against the question.

checklist.t: Title every chart with its point
checklist.d: "Revenue is flat while units grow", not "Revenue and units".
Every dashboard needs "as of" and where the data came from, visibly.

stages.title: Write the one-pager
stages.description: Question, method, finding, caveat. This is the thing you send; the dashboard is the thing they click afterwards.

checklist.t: Lead with the finding and its number
checklist.d: First line, no build-up.
Source, N, what you did. Enough to be checkable.
The chart that makes the point alone.
What this does not show, and what you would look at next.

stages.title: Read the prompt and the rubric like a judge
stages.description: The rubric tells you where the marks are. Reading it first is the cheapest advantage in any competition.

checklist.d: Slide limit, format, time limit, what must be addressed. Tick them off at the end.

checklist.t: Write the weighting next to each section
checklist.d: Then allocate your hours in the same proportion.
Prompts bury it in two pages of context. Teams answer the context.

checklist.t: Split the work by section, with a merge time
checklist.d: And agree who owns the final deck.

stages.title: Size the opportunity
stages.description: A number, built from stated assumptions, defensible to within an order of magnitude. Judges care far more about the build than the answer.

checklist.d: If they disagree by more than 2x, one of your assumptions is wrong.

checklist.t: Show the assumptions on the slide
checklist.d: Judges mark the logic. A naked number invites the worst question.
From an annual report or official statistic. One real anchor makes the rest credible.
If your market is bigger than the industry, start again.

stages.title: Build the financial case
stages.description: A small model: revenue build, cost, investment, and a payback or NPV. Simple and auditable beats elaborate and unexplainable.

checklist.d: Nobody believes year seven, and defending it wastes your Q&A.
So you can change an assumption live when a judge challenges it.
Payback period, NPV or incremental margin. One, on the recommendation slide.
Have the pessimistic number ready before anyone asks for it.

stages.title: Pick one recommendation and commit
stages.description: The single biggest differentiator. Judges reward a defended choice over a balanced survey every time.

checklist.d: What to do, and what it is worth.
Each one traceable to a slide of analysis.

checklist.t: Name the alternatives and why they lose
checklist.d: One line each. Pre-empts the obvious challenge.
Ninety days, six months, year one. Owners named.

stages.title: Build the deck
stages.description: Action titles, one idea per slide, the chart as the argument. Read the titles in order — they should be the whole case.

checklist.t: Write all the titles first, as claims
checklist.d: Then build the slide that proves each one.

checklist.t: Read the titles aloud in sequence
checklist.d: If they do not tell the story on their own, the structure is wrong.
Grey everything except the bar that makes the point.
Slide count, format, mandatory sections. Then check again.

stages.title: Rehearse the Q&A, not the pitch
stages.description: The pitch you can control. The questions decide it. Prepare the attacks on your own weakest assumption.

checklist.d: Including transitions. Overrunning is an unforced error.
Start from your own assumptions. Assign an owner to each.

checklist.t: Know which appendix slide answers what
checklist.d: "Slide 19" said calmly is worth several marks.
Who answers what, and how you hand a question across without talking over each other.

stages.title: Decide what the model is for
stages.description: A model answers one question. Naming it decides the structure, the granularity and when you are finished.

checklist.t: Write the question in one sentence
checklist.d: "What is this business worth at a 12% discount rate?" or "Can it service the debt through FY27?"

checklist.t: Name the output that answers it
checklist.d: A valuation range, a DSCR by year, a payback period. Build towards that cell.
Monthly for cash and covenants, annual for valuation. Mixing them is a rebuild.

checklist.t: Decide what you will not model
checklist.d: Write the exclusions down. They are the honest answer to "why isn't X in here?"

stages.title: Lay the workbook out before typing a number
stages.description: Tab structure, one timeline, colour convention and the checks tab — set up now, or retrofitted painfully later.

checklist.d: Cover, Inputs, Workings, Outputs, Checks. In that order, every time.

checklist.t: Put the timeline in one row and reference it everywhere
checklist.d: Period end dates across the top, same column for the same period on every sheet.
Blue hardcoded inputs, black formulas, green on-sheet links. Write the key on the cover.
Three labelled rows waiting for formulas, so you cannot forget to add them.

stages.title: Build the historicals from the filings
stages.description: Three years of actuals, typed from a real source, tying to the published statements to the rupee or dollar.

checklist.d: The last three annual reports or 10-Ks from EDGAR or the company's investor page.
Not a paste from a data provider you cannot check. Typing is where you notice the restatements.
Your revenue, EBITDA and net income must equal the published figures. Fix your sheet, not the source.
Margins, working capital days, capex as a percentage of revenue. These become your forecast drivers.

stages.title: Forecast the operations
stages.description: Revenue and cost built from drivers you can defend, not a growth percentage typed over the top.

checklist.d: Volume and price, or customers and ARPU. One blended growth rate is not a model.
Variable as a percentage of revenue, fixed as a value that grows with inflation.
If your forecast margin leaves the historical range, you need a reason in writing.
Receivable, inventory and payable days driving the balances, not plugged numbers.

checklist.t: Add the capex and depreciation schedule
checklist.d: Opening, additions, depreciation, closing — tying to both the balance sheet and the cash flow.

stages.title: Close the loop and make it balance
stages.description: Debt schedule, interest, and the circularity that comes with them — handled with a circuit breaker rather than iterative calculation left on.

checklist.d: Opening, drawdown, repayment, closing, with interest on the average balance.
A switch that replaces the circular interest with a hardcode, so you can always break a stuck model.
Assets minus liabilities minus equity equals zero, in every single period.
Closing cash on the cash flow statement equals cash on the balance sheet. No exceptions.

checklist.t: Turn the checks red on purpose
checklist.d: Break something deliberately and confirm the checks tab catches it.

stages.title: Value it
stages.description: The output the question asked for, built off the cash flows you just forecast.

checklist.t: Derive free cash flow from the statements
checklist.d: Not from a separate assumption block — it has to fall out of the model you built.
Cost of equity and cost of debt, each with its inputs sourced on the inputs tab.
Perpetuity growth and exit multiple, and show both so the reader can pick.
If your DCF value implies a multiple nothing in the sector trades at, say why.

stages.title: Sensitise it, then audit it
stages.description: A single number invites one question. A range with named drivers answers it in advance.

checklist.d: Flex the two assumptions the answer actually moves on, and present the grid.
Rank the drivers by how much they swing the answer. This is the slide people remember.

checklist.t: Trace three formulas end to end
checklist.d: Pick three output cells and follow every precedent back to an input. Fix what surprises you.

checklist.t: Hand it to someone else to break
checklist.d: Give them the workbook with no explanation and watch where they get confused.
Answer, range, three assumptions, one chart.

stages.title: Decide the ask before the story
stages.description: How much, for how long, against which milestone. Everything in the deck argues for this number.

checklist.t: Work out the runway you need
checklist.d: Monthly burn times the months to the next milestone, plus a margin. Not a round number you liked.
"₹2Cr ARR" or "regulatory approval in two states". Vague milestones get vague answers.

checklist.t: Break the use of funds into three lines
checklist.d: Usually people, go-to-market, and product. With headcount numbers.
At a plausible valuation, what share does this round cost you? Know it before you are asked.

stages.title: Write the story as ten sentences
stages.description: The narrative first, in plain text. If the sentences do not follow one another, the deck will not either.

checklist.d: Ten or twelve lines, in order, in a plain document. No design yet.
Each should follow from the last. Where you have to explain a jump, a slide is missing.

checklist.t: Cut any sentence that does not advance the ask
checklist.d: Interesting and irrelevant is the most common deck failure.
Have them read only the sentences and tell you what the company does and what you want.

stages.title: Build the market from the bottom up
stages.description: A number you derive on the slide, from units you can name — not a share of someone else's headline figure.

checklist.d: Number of businesses or people who could buy, from a registry, census or industry body.

checklist.t: Multiply by what they would spend
checklist.d: Your price, or what they spend on the workaround today.

checklist.t: Show the arithmetic on the slide
checklist.d: Three numbers and an equals sign. It is more convincing than a bigger number with no derivation.
If the published market size is ten times yours, find out which definition differs.

stages.title: Build the traction slide honestly
stages.description: The chart that goes up, with the axis labelled and the period named. Small and specific beats big and vague.

checklist.t: Pick the one metric that means it works
checklist.d: Paying customers, weekly active users, revenue. One line, not a dashboard.

checklist.t: Label the axes and the period
checklist.d: An unlabelled up-and-to-the-right chart is read as hiding something.

checklist.t: Add the cohort view to the appendix
checklist.d: Retention by signup month is the question that follows the growth chart.
"Pre-revenue, 40 pilot users" is a position. A dressed-up version of it is a liability.

stages.title: Build the business model and unit economics
stages.description: What you charge, what serving costs, and what a customer is worth — with the model behind it ready to send.

checklist.t: State the pricing in one line
checklist.d: Per seat, per transaction, per month. With the actual number on the slide.

checklist.t: Compute gross margin from real costs
checklist.d: Including the ones people forget: payment fees, support time, infrastructure.

checklist.t: Show CAC and payback if you have them
checklist.d: If you do not, say so and show the pilot cost of acquiring the users you have.

checklist.t: Put the three-year model in the appendix
checklist.d: Three years, driver-based, with the assumptions on their own tab.

stages.title: Design it so it reads without you
stages.description: Most first reads are silent and on a phone. Design for that, not for the room.

checklist.t: Put the claim in the title of every slide
checklist.d: Read the titles in order — they should be the whole pitch.

checklist.t: Cut the word count by half
checklist.d: Then check each slide is legible at thumbnail size.

checklist.t: Use one chart per slide, highlighted
checklist.d: Grey everything except the line that makes the point.

checklist.t: Open the PDF on a phone
checklist.d: If you cannot read the axis labels, nor can the investor on their commute.

stages.title: Rehearse the questions, not the pitch
stages.description: You control the twelve slides. The twenty minutes after them decide the meeting.

checklist.t: Deliver it in under ten minutes, timed
checklist.d: Twice, out loud. Most first meetings give you less time than you planned for.
Start from your weakest slide. Market size, churn, why the incumbents don't do this.

checklist.t: Know which appendix slide answers each
checklist.d: Being able to say "slide 19" and go straight there is worth a lot.
Usually "what if Google does this?". Have a real answer, not a deflection.

stages.title: Pick a task worth automating
stages.description: Frequent, rule-based and annoying. Rare or judgement-heavy tasks cost more to automate than they save.

checklist.d: From your own week or your team's. Note how often each happens.
With a stopwatch, honestly. Estimates are always wrong in the flattering direction.
Pick the highest. A ten-minute daily task beats a two-hour quarterly one.
If the right action depends on judgement every time, automate the steps around the judgement instead.

stages.title: Map the process as it actually runs
stages.description: Every step, including the ones nobody documented. This is where you find out half of them are unnecessary.

checklist.d: Including opening the tab, copying the field, renaming the file. The invisible steps are the work.
Handoffs between people are where the delay lives, and often where the automation pays.
Anywhere a human chooses. Those stay human, at least to begin with.
Removing a step beats automating it. Do that before touching a tool.

stages.title: Build the happy path only
stages.description: Trigger, three steps, one output, working end to end. Edge cases come after something works.

checklist.d: A schedule, a new row, an incoming email, a form submission. One trigger, clearly defined.

checklist.t: Build three steps and test each
checklist.d: Run after every step rather than building the whole chain and debugging it blind.

checklist.t: Use the tool's secret store for credentials
checklist.d: Never paste a key or password into a step's field.

checklist.t: Run it on real data once, read-only
checklist.d: Have it report what it would do before letting it write anything.

stages.title: Add the AI step, if it earns its place
stages.description: Classification, extraction or drafting — where a rule would be brittle. With a check on the output, not blind trust.

checklist.d: Categorise this email, pull the amount out of this invoice, draft this reply. One narrow job.

checklist.t: Write the prompt with the output format pinned
checklist.d: Ask for JSON with named fields, so the next step can rely on the shape.

checklist.t: Test it on twenty real examples
checklist.d: Count how many it got right. Below about 90% it needs a human review step, not a fix.
What happens when the model returns something unparseable. It will.

stages.title: Make it fail loudly
stages.description: The difference between an automation people trust and one they quietly stop relying on.

checklist.d: On failure, post to a channel someone reads, with the step name and the input that broke it.
Transient network failures retry; a malformed input should not retry forever.
Feed it bad input and confirm you hear about it within minutes.
Append each run to a sheet with a timestamp and outcome, so you can see it is still alive.

stages.title: Measure it and hand it over
stages.description: The saved hours are the CV line, and the handover note is what keeps it running after you.

checklist.t: Run both processes for a week
checklist.d: Manual and automated side by side, so you can prove the output matches.
Timed manual duration times frequency, minus the minutes the automation needs. One number.
What it does, how to change it, how to switch it off, and who owns it now.

checklist.t: Move it to the team's account
checklist.d: An automation running on your personal login is a liability, not a deliverable.

stages.title: Write the objective as a verb
stages.description: Not "introduction to X" — what can they do at 5pm that they couldn't at 2pm, and how would you know.

checklist.t: Write one sentence starting "By the end, each person can…"
checklist.d: A verb and an object: build a pivot table from a raw export; run a structured interview.
The thing they produce in the room that shows it worked.

checklist.t: Find out what they already know
checklist.d: Ask three attendees beforehand. Pitching at the wrong level is the commonest failure.
Two objectives in ninety minutes means neither lands.

stages.title: Design it as activities, not slides
stages.description: Build the run sheet backwards from the objective, with at least half the clock given to the room.

checklist.d: Take an existing play with timings rather than inventing a structure from nothing.

checklist.t: Write the run sheet in minutes
checklist.d: Segment, duration, who talks, what the room does. It must add up to the time you have.
If you are talking for more than half of it, convert a segment into an exercise.

checklist.t: Plan the first five minutes exactly
checklist.d: Word for word. It sets whether the room participates at all.

stages.title: Build the materials, worksheet first
stages.description: The worksheet is what the room actually uses. Slides are a backdrop, and fewer is better.

checklist.d: The task, the inputs, what to produce, how long. Self-contained.
Half-filled, so the room starts doing rather than staring at a blank page.
One per segment, as signposts. If a slide carries content, it belongs on the worksheet.
One completed version you can show when the room gets stuck — not before.

stages.title: Pilot it on two people
stages.description: An hour with two colleagues finds the broken brief and the segment that runs twice as long as planned.

checklist.d: The part most likely to fail. Hand them the brief and stay silent.

checklist.t: Time it against your run sheet
checklist.d: Expect the exercise to take 1.5x what you planned. Adjust the sheet, not the exercise.

checklist.t: Note every question they asked you
checklist.d: Each one is a sentence missing from the brief.

checklist.t: Cut a quarter of the content
checklist.d: Whatever survives the pilot without being missed was never needed.

stages.title: Run it
stages.description: Hold the timings, let the room work, and resist filling silence with more explanation.

checklist.t: Open with the objective and the finish time
checklist.d: In the first minute. People participate more when they know the shape.

checklist.t: Start the exercise earlier than feels comfortable
checklist.d: Within the first twenty minutes. Momentum comes from doing.

checklist.t: Keep to the run sheet out loud
checklist.d: "Five minutes left on this." It keeps the room moving and you honest.
Each person writes the one thing they will do differently, and reads it out.

checklist.t: Collect the feedback before they leave
checklist.d: Three questions, on paper or a phone link, in the room.

stages.title: Write up what happened
stages.description: What they could do afterwards, what the feedback said, and what you would change — the part that makes it a CV line.

checklist.d: How many people produced the thing the objective named. That is the result.
Including the segment people rated worst. You will run this again.

checklist.t: Send the takeaway within a day
checklist.d: The one-pager plus anything you promised in the room, while it is still warm.

checklist.t: Write the three changes for next time
checklist.d: Specific edits to the run sheet, not resolutions.
